newsitem.title: UK: German stocks lead European bourses decline.
newsitem.headline: German stocks lead European bourses decline.

text.p: European stock and bond markets went into retreat on Thursday after investors sold Wall Street down, Frankfurt headed the decline with losses of about two percent.
London and Paris dropped, too, but the falls were nowhere as bad as Frankfurt and prices began to inch back up during the morning.

On the currency front, the dollar opened in Europe below 1.70 marks for the first time in almost two weeks, but steadied above 1.69 as traders scaled back expectations of an imminent U.S. interest rate rise and reassessed German economic strength.
A selloff in high technology stocks and bonds was mainly behind the 45 point fall in the Dow Jones Industrial Average to 7,039 points overnight, which followed two consecutive record highs.

Although the U.S. Federal Reserve's Beige Book showed price pressures under control on Wednesday, the U.S. bond market remained nervous about inflation -- reflected in early weakness in the British and German government bond markets.
That added to selling pressure in equity markets, although traders cited Wall Street's performance as the major factor in declining share prices that also saw Tokyo's Nikkei index shed 1.56 percent.
Share and bond markets were likely to focus later on U.S. retail sales data, due at 1330 GMT, for signs whether a robust U.S. economy could prompt a rate rise.
Fears the U.S. Federal Reserve may be tempted to make a pre-emptive strike on U.S. inflation by raising interest rates at the end of the month worried investors on both sides of the Atlantic.
"The odds are heavily in favour of a pre-emptive rate rise this time," said Robin Aspinall, strategist at National Australia Bank.

Although the Fed's "Beige Book" report showed few signs of accelerating inflation, a growing number of market watchers believe the Fed may slip in a small rate hike after the March 25 meeting of the Federal Open Markets Committee.
The early two percent fall in German bourse trade was blamed on the market catching up with Wednesday's losses in IBIS screen-based business, Wall Street and the drop in the dollar.
But traders said later the market could be moving into a consolidation phase following its recent strong rally.
Hoechst tumbled for the third day on disappointment that it was dropping a plan to list its HMR drugs unit. It was down 75 pfennigs at 69.7 marks by 1200 GMT but well off its lows.
Lufthansa fell 45 pfennigs to 24.05 marks after the airline reported late on Wednesday lower 1996 profits and the sale of its stake in Lauda Air.

Traders in London said the FTSE 100 index's early losses echoed similar falls on Wednesday, although they did not expect a significant pull-back and the blue-chip FTSE later came off its lows. The FTSE 100 was down 10.6 points to 4,411.9 by 1215 GMT.
Enterprise bucked the weaker market trend, jumping 23-1/2p to 657, after the company increased its dividend more than most analysts had forecast and raised its production estimates for 1999.
In Paris, French shares showed resilience by clawing back some of the ground lost during the morning on worries over possible interest rate tightening.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index was down 4.07 points, or 0.15 percent, at 2,637.63 at 1215 GMT, while the CAC-40 futures contract was down 9.5 at 2,647 from Wednesday's close.
Suez eased 1.2 percent and Lyonnaise des Eaux fell 1.85 percent after Belgian ministers attacked any possible merger move between the two groups, as they would hurt Tractebel and Belgian interests.
On foreign exchange markets analysts said a generalised paring of high-yield currency positions in Europe was tending to boost lower-yield currencies, benefiting the Swiss franc.

By the European mid-session the mark and Swiss franc were firm against other major currencies, although traders said Swiss franc strength was related more to an adjustment of capital flows rather than any fresh view of Swiss interest rates or the economy.

"At least part of what's happened over the past week has been a reassessment of the gloom about the German economy. The latest round of data was a warning that German rates will not stay this low forever," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at JP Morgan in Europe.
CURRENCIES AT 1215 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.6942 marks and 122.75 yen, compared with 1.7023 marks and 122.62 yen in late trading on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1215 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was down 10.6 points, or 0.24 percent, at 4,411.9.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was down 44.07, or 0.15 percent, at 2,637.63.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was down 63.35 points, or 1.85 percent, at 3,352.05.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold fixed at $351.45 up five cents. Palladium fell $3.00 from $152.75, while silver was down a cent at $5.23.
